desc:
A marketing attribution review for online stores shows which channels bring real orders and which only collect credit. Ecom Swift LLC compares your analytics, ad accounts, email tool and store, then writes a short report with clear next steps.

## What is marketing attribution, and why is it so often wrong?

Marketing attribution is the practice of assigning credit for an order to the channels that helped bring it. It is often wrong because every tool counts in its own way. An ad platform claims an order if the shopper saw or clicked its ad within a set window, while your email tool claims the same order if the shopper opened a message. Add them up and the total can pass what your store actually sold.

None of the tools is lying. Each one only sees its own slice of the journey, and each has a reason to show itself in a good light. A review puts those slices side by side and checks them against the one number you can trust: the orders in your store.

## How attribution changes where your budget goes

Budget follows credit. If a retargeting campaign claims every order from visitors who were already about to buy, you will keep funding it and starve the channels that found those visitors in the first place. If a search campaign looks weak because it starts journeys that finish elsewhere, you may cut the very thing that fills the top of your funnel.

Seeing the difference between last-click and first-click paths helps you separate channels that close orders from channels that start them. Splitting new and returning customers shows whether a channel finds people or just reminds people who already know you. Better decisions about spend usually come from understanding these roles, not from chasing one perfect number.

## What a useful attribution review includes

- A list of every channel that sends traffic or orders, including organic search, paid search, paid social, email and direct.
- Last-click orders and revenue per channel, pulled from Google Analytics.
- Each ad platform's own claimed results, set beside what the store recorded.
- First-click and assisted paths, so you see which channels begin journeys.
- A note on tracking gaps, such as missing campaign tags or traffic labeled direct by mistake.
- A split between new and returning customers where the data allows.
- Cost per order by channel, using spend you give us.
- A plain verdict for each channel: keep, test, fix or reduce.
- Suggested budget moves with the reasons written out.

## How we run the review

First we ask which channels you use and collect read access to your analytics, your ad accounts, your email platform and your store. We never ask for passwords, since collaborator or viewer roles are enough for reading data.

We then export orders from the store and compare them with what Analytics and each ad platform report for the same dates. Differences are expected, so we explain them: overlapping attribution windows, blocked scripts, untagged links and cross-device journeys all play a part. Where a gap points to a real tracking fault, we list it.

Next we build the channel table and write our honest view of each row. The Basic package covers a handful of channels on last-click data. Standard adds first-click paths and a comparison with ad platform claims. Premium adds the customer split, cost per order, budget suggestions, two simple tests and a call to talk it through. The result is a short report you can act on the same week.

## Do and avoid

**Do:**
- Give us honest spend figures for every channel, including agency fees.
- Tag your campaign links the same way every time.
- Compare any platform's claims with your store's order list.
- Treat the report as a guide for small tests, not a final ruling.
- Review again after any big change in budget or tracking.

**Avoid:**
- Trusting one tool as the only source of truth.
- Cutting a channel in one move without a test.
- Counting direct traffic as a channel that needs no explanation.
- Mixing paid and organic results under one label.
- Reading too much into a short period with few orders.

## Who an attribution review is for

It suits owners who spend on two or more channels and feel unsure which one deserves the next dollar. It also helps stores where Meta, Google and email each claim a large share of sales that add up to more than the store shows. A brand preparing a budget for a busy season can use the report to decide where to test first.

No review makes attribution exact. What it gives you is a clearer, more honest picture and a short list of next steps.

## What we need from you

A list of the channels you use, the date range you want reviewed, and viewer or collaborator access to your analytics, ad accounts, email tool and store. If you track spend in a sheet, send that too. A short note about promotions, price changes or stock problems in the period helps us explain odd weeks. If your tracking is messy, say so: we will note the gaps and tell you what to repair first.
